confidence_note: Newport defines digital minimalism as a philosophy of technology use in which you focus your online time on a small number of carefully selected and optimized activities that strongly support things you value, and then happily miss out on everything else. He criticizes the 'any-benefit' mindset: adopting a tool if it offers any benefit at all, ignoring its costs. He illustrates a more deliberate approach with the Amish, who, contrary to stereotype, don't reject all technology but ask whether a new technology will serve or harm their community's values before adopting it. The reference TR text's framing of the two questions is consistent with this.
facts: Newport defines digital minimalism as a philosophy in which you focus your online time on a small number of carefully selected and optimized activities that strongly support things you value, and happily miss out on everything else.
He criticizes the 'any-benefit' approach: justifying a tool because it offers some benefit, without weighing its costs in time and attention.
The better question is whether a tool is the best way to support something you deeply value.

He uses the Amish as an example: they don't reject all technology, but carefully evaluate whether each new tool will strengthen or weaken the values of their community before adopting it, sometimes with restrictions.
He argues that clutter is costly: many small tools, each with small benefits, together take a large share of our time and attention.
Minimalists are comfortable missing out on small benefits in exchange for protecting what matters most.
tension: Almost every app has some benefit. So why do so many people feel worse with all of them combined?
opening_idea: Ask whether an app has any benefit, and the answer is almost always yes. Newport says that's the wrong question.

lessons.idea: Ask whether it's the best way to serve a deep value.

reflect: Which tool do you use just because it has 'some' benefit?
What deep value is each of your main apps supposed to serve?
reflect_final: Which app would you keep if it had to prove it's the best way to serve something you truly value?

use_cases.situation: You're about to install another productivity app.
use_cases.move: Ask what value it serves and whether it's the best way to serve it.

use_cases.situation: Your team adopts every new tool someone suggests.
use_cases.move: Agree on a rule: new tools must replace something or clearly serve a core goal.

use_cases.situation: Your teenager wants a new social app.
use_cases.move: Talk together about what it would add and what it might cost.

pocket_idea: Don't ask if a tool has any benefit; ask if it's the best way to serve what you value.

conversation_variants.punchline_idea: Almost every app has some benefit, which is exactly why 'any benefit' is the wrong test.
conversation_variants.thirty_sec_idea: Definition of digital minimalism, any-benefit mindset, the Amish example.
